theme: Isaiah’s call; Immanuel, God with us
readingInstruction: Read Isaiah 6:1-8:22. Chapter 6 is the call vision, one of the most important scenes in the Bible. Read it slowly, then continue into chapter 7, where Isaiah gives King Ahaz the sign of Immanuel.
settingTheScene: Isaiah has a vision of God in the year King Uzziah died, about 740 BC. Uzziah had reigned for fifty-two years, a time of stability, and his death left a sense of insecurity. In chapters 7 and 8, the setting shifts to the crisis of 734 BC, when Syria and Israel allied against Judah and threatened King Ahaz. Isaiah goes out to meet Ahaz and offers him a sign.
observation: “In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple” (6:1).
“Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!” (6:3).
“Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips” (6:5).
“Behold, this has touched your lips; your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for” (6:7).
“If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all” (7:9).
“Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel” (7:14).
“To the teaching and to the testimony! If they will not speak according to this word, it is because they have no light of dawn” (8:20).
interpretation:
Isaiah’s vision is the pattern of all true encounters with God. First, God is seen in majesty: seated on a throne, the hem of his robe filling the temple. Seraphim cover their faces and their feet and cry, “Holy, holy, holy.” The threefold repetition is the strongest superlative in Hebrew. Holiness is the one attribute of God that is repeated this way in Scripture. It means that God is utterly set apart, pure, and other. The doorposts shake and the house fills with smoke.

Second, the response is a recognition of sin. “Woe is me! For I am lost.” Isaiah, a respected man, a prophet who had already pronounced woes on others, now sees himself. The nearer one comes to God’s holiness, the clearer one’s own uncleanness becomes.

Third, there is cleansing. A seraph takes a burning coal from the altar and touches his mouth: “Your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for.” Isaiah does not clean himself. God provides the atonement, through the altar, a picture of sacrifice.

Fourth, the commission. Only now does God ask, “Whom shall I send?” And Isaiah, forgiven, says, “Here I am! Send me.” Service follows grace. The message he is given is a hard one: the people will hear and not understand, until the land is laid waste. Yet “the holy seed” is the stump that remains.

In chapter 7 the lesson is applied to a king. Ahaz is afraid. Isaiah tells him to be calm and trust. When Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign, with a pious excuse, God gives one anyway: a virgin will conceive and bear a son, Immanuel, “God with us.” In the immediate setting, a child would be born as a sign that the enemy kings would fall before he grew up. Yet the language reaches beyond. The promise is that God himself will be with his people.
connection: John 12:41 says that Isaiah saw Jesus’ glory and spoke of him. Matthew 1:22-23 quotes Isaiah 7:14 as fulfilled in the virgin birth of Jesus. Revelation 4:8 echoes the seraphim, “Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty.” Romans 10:15 asks, “How are they to preach unless they are sent?” 1 Peter 2:8 quotes Isaiah 8:14 about the stone of stumbling.
application:
Spend a few minutes in silence before God’s holiness. Let it correct how small your view of him has been.

Confess one sin by name, and receive the cleansing God has provided in Christ.

Pray Isaiah’s words, “Here I am! Send me,” and ask where God may be sending you.
prayerPrompts: Praise God as holy, holy, holy, in your own words.
Confess your unclean lips, and thank him for taking away your guilt.
Tell him, “Here I am,” and listen.
